reason: Gravity is a plausible way to bring about the star's collapse and release its matter, though this is a guess.
expectation: The star will change or release matter as gravity acts on it.

alternatives.reason: Checking the star's available ingredients would clarify the intended interaction.

effect: Gravity made a massive star by gathering more gas, rather than immediately causing its collapse. The star may need another interaction to return its matter.
reaction: The shorter lifetime of a more massive star is an interesting consequence.
reason: Inspecting the massive star should reveal which available ingredients can advance its transformation.
expectation: The inspection will show possible partners for the star, or automatically perform the interaction if there is only one.

effect: Fire automatically transformed the massive star into a fusing core, revealing how it makes heavier elements before returning matter.
reaction: The link between fusion and new elements is satisfying, though Fire is a mythic shorthand.
reason: Inspecting the fusing core should reveal how to advance toward releasing the star's matter.
expectation: The inspection will list compatible partners and automatically combine if only one operation is available.

effect: Earth advanced the fusing core to heavy elements, which are still inside the star and need to be scattered.
reaction: The distinction between making elements and dispersing them makes the sequence clearer.
reason: Inspecting the heavy elements should reveal how to release them from the star.
expectation: The inspection will show compatible partners and automatically combine if only one operation is available.

effect: Gravity triggered a supernova, scattering the star's outer layers; the released matter may need a further step to complete the goal.
reaction: The distinction that not every star ends this way is useful.
reason: Inspecting the supernova should reveal how to collect or use its scattered matter.
expectation: The inspection will show its available partners and automatically combine if only one operation is available.

effect: Air transformed the supernova into an expanding remnant; the goal has not yet been reported complete.
reaction: The expanding aftermath is a natural continuation, though its next use is not yet clear.
reason: Inspecting the remnant should reveal how to advance the release of the star's matter.
expectation: The inspection will list compatible partners and automatically combine if only one operation is available.

effect: The remnant can combine with either Fire or Heavy elements, so there is a meaningful choice rather than an automatic next step.
reaction: I'm curious whether the heavy elements will become part of a new cloud.
reason: Combining the remnant with Heavy elements seems the most direct way to return the star's material to space.
expectation: The heavy elements will mix into the expanding stellar debris.

alternatives.reason: Fire is also compatible, but its purpose is less clear to me.

effect: The remnant and heavy elements became enriched dust, suggesting the star's material is now dispersed but has not yet completed the goal.
reaction: The dust feels like a promising bridge to new worlds.
reason: Inspecting the enriched dust should reveal how to advance the star's returned matter.
expectation: The inspection will list compatible partners and automatically combine if only one operation is available.

effect: Gravity gathered the enriched dust into a new stellar nursery, completing the goal and connecting the star's death to ingredients for future rocky worlds.
reaction: That cycle was a satisfying payoff to the sequence.

mostWorthwhile.text: Making the stellar nursery was the most worthwhile moment: it gave the scattered material a clear future and made destruction feel like part of a larger cycle.

leastWorthwhile.text: The repeated inspections of objects with only one available partner felt somewhat mechanical, even though they moved the story forward.

surprise.text: I expected gravity to cause collapse immediately, but it first gathered gas into a more massive, shorter-lived star.

arbitrary.text: Earth producing heavy elements felt like symbolic shorthand rather than an intuitive physical action, though the explanation clarified the fusion it represented.

continue.text: Yes. The nursery's promise of future rocky worlds makes me curious to see how the world develops, although I would hope for more choices than the mostly automatic sequence here.
